critique.good: The whole comparison fits at first sight, and the option names and verdicts remain recognizable.
critique.problems: The paired assessment columns are cramped, making rows very tall and difficult to scan across. The Weaknesses header and several prose words split mid-word.
critique.cause: The 99px and 100px assessment columns leave only 78px and 79px for text; the latter is narrower than the Weaknesses header itself.

critique.good: The headers and words stay intact, and the paired assessments have comparable, readable space. The shorter rows make comparison easier.
critique.problems: The reader must scroll to see the full weaknesses and verdict; the verdict is outside the initial viewport. Some prose still wraps into many short lines.
critique.cause: The 145px and 155px assessment columns improve reading but bring the table to 484px, 124px beyond the viewport.

critique.good: The prose has a comfortable line length, words stay intact, and the relatively short rows make each comparison feel cohesive.
critique.problems: Much of the comparison, including nearly all weaknesses and the verdict, lies beyond the first view. The large horizontal scroll makes it harder to connect the conclusion with the option.
critique.cause: The 210px and 230px assessment columns, together with the 136px option column, produce a 650px table.

critique.good: The option names and headers remain intact, and the two assessment columns have enough space for reasonably natural prose. Strengths and weaknesses read as a balanced pair.
critique.problems: The verdict sits beyond the initial viewport, so readers must scroll to see the conclusion for each option. The rows are still fairly tall.
critique.cause: The 130px and 145px assessment columns make the table 79px wider than the viewport; the 73px verdict column is positioned at the far right.

critique.good: Nearly the whole table is visible initially, including most of the verdict column. Headers and words remain intact, and the paired assessment columns have similar widths.
critique.problems: The prose forms narrow, fragmented columns, making rows very tall and comparisons harder to follow. The verdict is still slightly outside the viewport.
critique.cause: The 102px and 111px assessment columns leave only 81px and 90px for text. Even with those tight widths, the four columns total 374px.

critique.good: The wider assessment columns produce more natural phrases and shorter rows. The option names are easy to scan, and strengths and weaknesses retain comparable prominence.
critique.problems: Much of the weaknesses column and the entire verdict require horizontal scrolling. Readers cannot see the full comparison at first sight.
critique.cause: The 155px and 170px assessment columns, together with the 100px option column, push the 73px verdict column well beyond the viewport.

critique.good: The paired assessment columns are reasonably balanced, and the option names and headers remain intact. The prose wraps at word boundaries.
critique.problems: The rows are tall, with especially ragged wrapping in Strengths. The verdict is mostly beyond the initial viewport, so the reader must scroll to see each conclusion.
critique.cause: The 120px Strengths and 130px Weaknesses widths leave limited room for prose, while their combined width pushes most of the 73px Verdict column beyond the viewport.

critique.good: This design brings more of Verdict into the initial viewport than the other two, while keeping words and headers intact.
critique.problems: The prose breaks into short fragments, making the second and third rows notably taller and harder to scan across. Verdict is still partly outside the viewport.
critique.cause: Reducing Strengths to 110px and Weaknesses to 120px saves only 20px of horizontal scrolling compared with r2A, but produces substantially more wrapping.

critique.good: The assessment prose has a more comfortable rhythm, and the shorter rows make comparisons easier to follow. Words and headers remain intact.
critique.problems: Verdict is entirely outside the initial viewport, and even the right edge of Weaknesses requires scrolling. The reader cannot see the full comparison at first sight.
critique.cause: The 140px and 150px assessment columns improve wrapping but push the 73px Verdict column well past the 360px viewport.

understanding.purpose: Compare framework options by their strengths, weaknesses, and overall verdict.
understanding.reading: Readers scan option names down the first column, then read across each row to weigh strengths against weaknesses and see the verdict. Wrapped prose can use the height created by the longer cell in the same row.
groups: Strengths and Weaknesses are paired qualitative assessments and need comparable space for reading across rows.
Option and Verdict frame each comparison: one identifies the choice and the other gives its conclusion.
keep_intact: Option names and verdicts should remain recognizable, with words kept intact where possible.
Column headers should remain legible, especially the paired Strengths and Weaknesses labels.
may_wrap: Strengths and weaknesses can wrap naturally at word boundaries.
Multiword option names can wrap between words.

bad.why: The narrow prose columns produce up to 11 lines per cell, making the rows tall and comparisons laborious for a saving of only 37px of horizontal scrolling relative to r2A.
It duplicates r1B and has the same excessively narrow prose columns and tall rows.

final.rationale: r2A gives the two prose columns similar visual weight, with a little more room for the longer weaknesses. Its option names and headers remain intact, and the row heights are manageable. The verdict column begins within the viewport, although its values require a short horizontal scroll; the table extends 51px beyond the viewport.

general: Columns with similar roles should have comparable visual weight, adjusted for differences in content length.
Horizontal scrolling can be worthwhile when it preserves intact words and makes dense prose easier to scan.
Row height matters because readers compare corresponding cells across each row.
specific: Strengths and weaknesses carry most of the content, while the short verdicts need much less width.
The 360px viewport cannot accommodate all four columns without splitting words, so every candidate requires some horizontal scrolling.

final.tradeoffs: r2B and r3B keep more of the verdict visible but have taller rows. r3C and r2C shorten the prose blocks further, at the cost of moving the verdict almost or entirely beyond the initial viewport.
final.uncertain: A designer who prioritizes reading the prose over seeing the verdict at first sight could reasonably prefer r3C or r2C. The width ranges are approximate: small changes can alter browser line breaks, so their equivalence would need a fresh render.

A.why: The option names and trade-off headers stay intact, but the narrow prose columns create many short lines and tall rows. The verdict sits at the viewport edge.

B.why: The wider trade-off columns make the prose easier to read and compare, with less vertical fragmentation. The verdict requires horizontal scrolling.

C.why: The headers and option names remain legible, but the two prose columns produce choppy line lengths and tall rows. The verdict is tight against the viewport edge.

D.why: Strengths and Weaknesses split in their headers, and words such as interactions and personalised break within cells. The wide verdict column takes space from the prose that needs it.

E.why: The wider prose columns give the text a comfortable rhythm and keep rows compact, but much of Weaknesses and the verdict lie beyond the initial viewport, making comparison dependent on scrolling.

F.why: The trade-off columns have a more useful balance than the squeezed layouts, and words remain largely intact. The verdict extends beyond the viewport and the prose still wraps frequently.

reviews.unsure: A and C appear identical at this scale. B and F are close: B gives the prose a little more room, while F keeps more of the verdict near the initial viewport.

A.why: The wider prose columns make rows relatively compact, but the viewport cuts through Weaknesses and leaves Verdict entirely offscreen, making comparison costly.

B.why: The two prose columns remain readable and balanced, but Verdict is mostly offscreen and the narrow columns produce tall rows.

C.why: All four columns are nearly visible at once, with words intact and a clear comparison between strengths and weaknesses. The prose columns are narrow, making rows tall.

D.why: The full comparison is nearly visible, words remain intact, and the prose columns have a consistent rhythm. Tall rows make scanning slower.

E.why: A little more room for the prose shortens the rows while keeping words intact. The Verdict column extends beyond the viewport, so its right edge requires a small scroll.

F.why: Although the table fits the viewport, both prose headers and many words split across lines, making the text and row comparisons difficult to read.

reviews.unsure: C and D look almost identical at this scale. E trades a small amount of horizontal scrolling for shorter rows; the preferred balance depends on how readily readers notice and use the scroll.
